title: Naive Prompt Optimization Beats the Fancy Search
hook: Prompt optimizers have grown elaborate search machinery. A single-lineage loop that just asks a teacher model to revise the prompt matches or beats GEPA with fewer rollouts.
key_points: Recent work has favoured increasingly complex prompt optimizers; the paper questions whether the complexity earns its keep.
NPO is a lightweight single-lineage method: iteratively revise the prompt with a teacher model using rollout feedback.
Matches or beats GEPA with fewer rollouts, and its advantage grows with stronger teacher models.
Suggests stronger teacher reasoning can partially substitute for optimizer-side search complexity.
In interactive games NPO stays broadly competitive with GEPA, while GRPO wins on some tasks less amenable to prompt optimization.
NPO-optimized prompts transfer verbatim to other student models, especially within the same family.
content_html: Prompt optimization is attractive because it can deliver fine-tuning-scale gains without touching weights — cheaper to run and cheaper to serve. In response, the field has produced increasingly sophisticated optimizers with population-based search, reflection trees, and multi-branch exploration. Chang and Chen ask whether the machinery is what's doing the work.
extra_html:
The method

Naive Prompt Optimization is deliberately plain: a single-lineage loop that iteratively revises one prompt using a teacher model and rollout feedback. No population, no branching search.

It matches or beats GEPA with fewer rollouts, and — the informative part — its advantage increases with stronger teacher models. The authors read this as a substitution: stronger teacher reasoning can partially replace optimizer-side search complexity. If the model doing the revising is smart enough, you do not need to search over many revisions.

Boundaries

In interactive games NPO remains broadly competitive with GEPA, but GRPO performs better on some tasks that are simply less amenable to prompt optimization — a useful reminder that the prompt is not always where the missing capability lives. NPO-optimized prompts also transfer verbatim to other student models, with the strongest transfer inside a model family.

The authors call the results preliminary. Taken at that level, the message is the familiar one: check the simple baseline before believing the complexity.

related.title: Sliding Window Beats Linear Attention
related.hook: The cheap baseline nobody bothered to run wins: sliding-window attention with sinks matches or beats retrofitted linear-attention models, and needs no post-training at all.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'single-lineage' mean in NPO, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back_html: It keeps one evolving prompt rather than maintaining and searching a population of candidates. That is what makes it cheap in rollouts — and it turns out not to cost much in quality.

flashcards.prompt: What substitution does the paper's teacher-strength result suggest?

choices.text: Stronger teacher reasoning can partially replace optimizer-side search complexity
More rollouts can replace a stronger teacher entirely
Prompt optimization can fully replace weight-level fine-tuning in all settings

flashcards.explanation_html: NPO's advantage over GEPA grows as the teacher gets stronger — the intelligence doing the revising substitutes for the machinery searching over revisions.

flashcards.prompt: Where does prompt optimization lose to GRPO?
flashcards.back_html: On interactive-game tasks less amenable to prompt optimization, where changing the weights beats changing the instructions.
